D:\\Proyectos\\video2-wt\\om500k\\vlog\\.text: See this little plastic valve in my fingers? It cost about $5. And it's one of the differences between an engine that dies at 200 ,000 miles and one that goes past 500 ,000. Same car, same engine, one owner sends it to the scrap yard at 130 ,000. The other one is still driving it at 500 ,000 with no big repairs. It's not luck, it's not the badge on the hood, it's six small habits. Last week, Doris asked me the question everybody asks, Claudio, Frank's car has 280 ,000 miles. How long can it really last? And when we opened Frank's old notebook, we found out he was already doing four of the six. The two he missed are the ones that kill most engines. I'll show you which. I'm Claudio. 35 years as a mechanic.

Most of these habits cost less than a tank of gas, and at the end, I'll give you the one sheet of paper that decides if your car makes it. Let's start in Doris's garage. Doris had been driving with her new key batteries for a week, happy as can be. Then her neighbor told her, "'At that mileage, you're living on borrowed time. Sell it before it dies on you.' She called me worried. "'Claudio, is he right? Is this car about to quit on me?' And I told her what I've seen for 35 years, engines don't die of old age. They die of dirt, heat, and neglect. The miles on the dash don't matter nearly as much as what happened during those miles.' So we sat in her garage with Frank's notebook, every oil change, every filter, every tire, written down in blue pen for 10 years. Reading that notebook, I could tell you exactly what kind of owner Frank was. A very good one with two blind spots.

Let me count down the 6 habits the way I showed Doris, the ones Frank did, and the 2 he didn't. Number 6. The first 5 minutes of every drive. When your engine sits overnight, the oil drains down into the pan. The first seconds after you start it, parts are turning with very little oil on them. That's when most engine wear happens. Not on the highway, in your driveway. A lot of people think the answer is to let it idle for 10 minutes to warm up. That's an old habit from carburetor days. Idling a cold engine for a long time actually makes it worse. It runs rich, it washes oil off the cylinder walls, and it takes forever to get warm. Here's what I do and what Frank did. Start it. Wait about 30 seconds while you put on your seatbelt and your glasses, then drive away gently.

No hard acceleration, stay under half the needle on the tachometer until the temperature gauge starts to move, and never ever floor it with a cold engine. Not pulling onto the highway, not because you're late. Cold oil is thick and it hasn't reached everything yet. And in winter, same rule, 30 seconds, then gentle. The engine warms up faster driving softly than sitting still. The only exception is scraping ice off the windshield. Do that first, because you need to see. One more for turbo engines. After a long hard drive, don't shut it off the second you park. Let it idle 30 seconds, the turbo spins hot, and the oil needs a moment to cool it down. Frank had written it in the front of his notebook, in capital letters, 30 seconds, then easy. Doris laughed. She said, he used to make me wait in the cold for 30 seconds, and I thought he was just being stubborn.

Number five, let your engine breathe. Every drop of air your engine burns goes through one paper filter first. It sits in a black plastic box under the hood about the size of a thin paperback book. A dirty air filter doesn't fail. It suffocates the engine slowly. You feel it as lazy acceleration, a tank of gas that doesn't go as far, sometimes a rough idle. People blame the gas or the weather. It's the filter. Pop the hood, find the big black plastic box, connect it to the large hose. Two to four metal clips hold the lid. Open them, lift the lid and pull the filter straight up. Now the test. Hold it up to the sun or to a flashlight. If light comes through the pleats, it's fine. If you can barely see light, it's done. Put the new one in the same way, seal side down and snap the clips. Five minutes, about $20.

And please, don't blow out a paper filter with compressed air and reuse it. You make tiny holes you can't see, and from that day on, the dirt goes straight into your engine. If you live on a gravel road or somewhere dusty, check it more often. I've pulled filters out of country cars that were brown as a paper bag after six months. Frank changed his every other oil change. Doris's was clean, she held it up to the garage light and said, look at that, I can see the light. I said, then Frank did his job. Number four, the cheapest habit on this list, free. Check your tire pressure once a month with a cold tire before you drive, a $10 gauge from any parts store, and rotate your tires every 5 ,000 to 7 ,000 miles, which is easy to remember if you do it with every oil change. This isn't just about tires.

A tyre 5lbs low wears the edges and it makes the whole front end work harder. Skip the rotation and the front tyres wear twice as fast and that uneven load hammers your ball joints, your bushings and your wheel bearings every single mile. Here's the part most people get wrong. The right number is not the one printed on the tyre, that's the tyre's maximum. Your number is on a sticker inside the driver's door frame. Open the door and look at the edge, that's the one. Unscrew the little cap on the valve, press the gauge on straight, read it. Low? Add air at the gas station a little at a time and check again. 3 minutes a wheel. And if your tyre pressure warning light comes on, don't just reset it and keep driving. A slow leak on the highway can ruin a tyre from the inside in a week. And a little rule for the seasons.

Your tyres lose about one pound of pressure for every 10 degrees the temperature drops. That's why the warning light so often comes on the first cold morning of fall. The tyre didn't break, the air got cold, check them and fill them up. In Frank's notebook, the first Saturday of every month, there was a little line. Tyres 32. 10 years of little lines. That's why Doris's front end was tight at 280 ,000 miles. I put all six habits with the exact numbers and a page to fill in on page 11 of my glovebox manual. It's trick number three in the book. But keep watching because the next two are the ones Frank missed. And I'll be straight with you, nobody pays me to say any of this. No oil company, no parts store, nobody. If that's the kind of help you want, subscribing costs you nothing and it keeps these coming every week. Number three.

The fluids that go bad on a calendar, not on the odometer. Most people think fluids only wear out with miles, two of them wear out with time even if the car sits in the garage. Brake fluid and coolant. Brake fluid pulls water out of the air, little by little through the hoses and the cap. After about two years, there's enough water in it to lower its boiling point and start corroding the inside of the brake system, including the most expensive part, the anti -lock brake unit. That part alone can cost a thousand dollars, almost every car maker says change it every two years, almost nobody does. Ask your shop for a brake fluid flush with the exact type your manual calls for, usually somewhere between a hundred and two hundred dollars. Some shops can even test the fluid for water with a little strip first.

Coolant is the coloured liquid in the plastic tank under the hood. Green, orange, pink or blue depending on your car. It carries heat away and it keeps the inside of the engine from rusting and it has a shelf life. Most cars, around 5 years, when it's old it turns rusty or brown and it starts eating the water pump, the radiator and the heater core. A small leak becomes overheating. Overheating becomes a head gasket. And a head gasket can cost more than the car is worth. Two rules. Use only the exact type your manual says. Don't mix colours because some of them turn into jelly together. And never, never open the radiator cap on a hot engine. It's under pressure and it can burn you badly. Look at the plastic tank instead. Engine cold. Here's how to look at your coolant safely. Engine cold, hood open. Find the plastic tank with the lines that say minimum and maximum.

The level should be between them, and the colour should be clear and bright, not rusty, not brown, not with anything floating in it. This is where Frank's notebook went quiet. Oil, tyres, filters, everyone. But brake fluid, never. And the last coolant entry was 8 years ago. Doris's coolant was the colour of weak coffee. We took it to a good independent shop that same week. Brake fluid, coolant, a new thermostat while they were in there. Under $400 together. That's what it costs to keep a 280 ,000 mile engine out of the scrap yard. Number 2, the $5 valve. Now, about this little valve I showed you at the start, it's called the PCV valve. Positive Crank Case Ventilation. Don't worry about the name. Here's what it does.

When your engine runs, a little bit of gas and pressure always sneaks past the pistons into the bottom of the engine. The PCV valve lets that pressure out and sends it back to be burned. It's how the engine breathes from the inside. When the valve clogs with sludge, the pressure has nowhere to go. So it pushes oil out wherever it can. The gaskets start leaking, the seals start weeping, and the engine starts using oil between changes. People think the engine is worn out. A lot of the time it's a $5 valve. On many engines, it's easy to find. A small valve pushed into a rubber grommet on top of the engine with a hose on it. Pull it out with the engine off and shake it. If it rattles, it's still moving. If it's silent or sticky with black goo, it needs to be replaced. Now, I'll be honest.

On some newer engines the valve is built into the engine cover and it's not a $5 job anymore. If you can't find it, ask your mechanic to check it at the next oil change. It takes them 2 minutes. My rule is to have it checked every 2 or 3 oil changes and replaced around every 50 ,000 miles, or sooner if the engine starts using oil. Frank never rode it down once. When I pulled Doris's out, it didn't rattle at all. It was stuck with black sludge. $7 at the parts store, 2 minutes to put in. And the small oil spot she'd been seeing under the car stopped growing. I had a customer once, a retired teacher, who was told her engine needed to be rebuilt because it was burning a quart of oil every month. Before she signed anything, we pulled the PCV valve, stuck shut, we put in a new one, and the oil use dropped to almost nothing. That was 11 years ago.

She still drives that car. Number one, the habit that decides if the other five ever happen. It's not a part, it's a notebook. Engine oil changed on a real schedule and written down every single time. Mileage, date, what oil, what filter. Every engine I've seen pass 500 ,000 miles belonged to someone who wrote things down, everyone. Because when you write it down, you don't forget, you don't guess, and you don't let a coupon or a little light on the dash decide for you. Here's how I set the schedule. Look in your manual for the severe service column like I showed you in the first video. For most people driving short trips, traffic and heat, that means somewhere around 5 ,000 miles with full synthetic oil. Highway drivers can go longer, your manual tells you, and don't trust that little oil lifelight alone.

On a lot of cars, it's set for perfect conditions, and perfect conditions don't exist on the way to church and the grocery store. Your notebook is the boss, the light is a reminder. Every oil change, write four things. The mileage, the date, the oil type, exactly what the cap or the manual says, and what was done besides the oil. Then write the mileage for the next one at the bottom, and set a reminder on your phone. And here's a bonus nobody tells you. The day you sell the car, that notebook is worth money. A buyer who sees 10 years of oil changes in blue pen pays more, and pays faster. Frank's notebook stopped three years ago when he got sick. Doris put it back in the glove box, and she wrote her first line under his last one. 280 ,412 miles. New brake fluid, new coolant, new PCV valve. In her own handwriting.

So here was Frank's score. Warming up gently, yes. The air filter, yes. Tires every month, yes. The notebook, yes. Four out of six. The fluids on the calendar and the little valve, no. And those two are exactly the ones that were starting to hurt his engine. Now, let me give you the whole thing as one simple routine. My six habits on one sheet of paper. Every drive, 30 seconds, then easy for five minutes. Every month, tire pressure, cold, with the number from the door sticker. Every oil change. Look at the air filter against the light. Rotate the tires. Write it all in the notebook. Every second or third change. Ask about the PCV valve. And on the calendar, not the odometer. Brake fluid every two years. Coolant around every five. Write those dates on the first page of the notebook, so you never have to remember them. And three mistakes I see all the time.

These are the expensive ones. Mistake one, believing the word lifetime. Some cars say the transmission fluid is lifetime fluid. Lifetime usually means the life of the warranty, not the life of the car. Ask your manual or a transmission shop about a drain and fill somewhere between 60 and 100 ,000 miles. Mistake two, on a high mileage transmission that's never been serviced, don't let anybody sell you a machine flush. It can push old dirt where it does damage. A gentle drain and fill, maybe done twice, is the safe way. Mistake three, ignoring an engine that starts using oil. Check the dipstick every thousand miles once the car is older. If it's dropping, check the PCV valve before anybody talks to you about a new engine. And a few quick questions people always ask me. Is full synthetic oil worth it? For most modern engines, yes. And many of them require it.

It handles heat better and it stays clean longer. Use exactly the grade your manual says. The numbers matter more than the brand. What about high mileage oil? It can help an older engine with small leaks because it has conditioners for the seals. It's not magic, but it's not a scam either. If your manual's grade is available in a high mileage version, it's a fine choice. My car already has a lot of miles and I never did any of this. Is it too late? No, start today. Every one of these habits helps from the day you start. Doris started at 280 ,000. What about the timing belt? Some engines have a rubber timing belt that must be replaced on schedule and some have a chain that usually lasts. Your manual tells you which one you have. If it's a belt, that's a shop job and you don't skip it. Do I have to go to the dealership to keep my warranty? In the United States, no.

You can use any good shop or do the work yourself as long as you use the right parts and fluids and keep the receipts. Another reason for the notebook. A few weeks later, Doris called me again. She said the car felt smoother, the oil spot under it was gone, and her neighbor had asked her who her mechanic was. And she told him, I don't need to sell it. Frank started it and I'm finishing it. 500 ,000 miles, Claudio, you promised. I didn't promise, but I told her the truth. With those six habits, that car has a real chance. And it already has the most important thing. Somebody who writes things down. If you want to check your own car before anybody hands you an estimate, I made a free guide called Before the Shop.
